A1.justification: Both PDFs describe J1 and contain readable main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The retained methods and experiments can be matched despite substantial reorganization and additional material in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of trained J1 models, including benchmark results, reward and prompt ablations, positional-bias analyses, and test-time scaling experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains original J1 experiments and adds Qwen-based and multitask results, decoding-sensitivity experiments, and a scalar reward-model comparison.

M1.justification: v1 develops separate pairwise and pointwise judges. v2 Section 2.3 adds MultiTask-J1, jointly training pairwise scoring and pointwise scoring in one model usable in either mode. This substantially extends the training procedure; the existing formulations and correctness/consistency rewards are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 22K training pairs from 17K WildChat and 5K MATH prompts and evaluate on PPE, RewardBench, RM-Bench, JudgeBench, and FollowBenchEval. The added model configurations, controls, and representative reasoning examples do not establish additional dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated Qwen3-32B and o3 baselines, numerous RewardBench comparators including Reward Reasoning Model, RM-R1, and CompassJudger, and a Bradley-Terry model trained on the same base model and data. Comparator membership also contracts in places: GPT-4o and DeepSeek-GRM MetaRM voting disappear from the PPE comparison, while the detailed RewardBench table drops EvalPlanner and DeepSeek-GRM rows.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the experimental configurations with Qwen3-32B, joint-versus-separate training comparisons, and a scalar-model control matching the base model and training data. Table 9 introduces greedy-versus-temperature-0.6 evaluation, and several tables add cross-benchmark Overall summaries. The original dataset sizes and benchmark-specific accuracy conventions remain; the PDFs do not establish reruns of retained Llama experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds multitask-versus-separate judge comparisons, decoding robustness, a matched-data scalar-model control, and three detailed reasoning case studies. Its score-distribution analysis concerns the multitask Qwen model rather than separate 8B judges. Existing reward, prompt, KL, and scaling analyses largely remain, although some detailed 8B and JudgeBench comparison entries are removed.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, v2 Table 9 reports sampling results over eight seeds with uncertainty values of ±0.1, and Section 4.1 reports p < 0.0001. These are limited additions to statistical reporting: the uncertainty statistic and significance-test procedure are unspecified, and the eight seeds concern inference sampling rather than documented repeated training.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new models and controls, including PPE Correctness scores of 74.6 for separate pairwise J1-Qwen-32B and 76.8 for its multitask counterpart. Most retained Llama benchmark scores match v1. Detailed PPE Preference and some 8B scaling entries disappear. The new scalar-control table contains unexplained J1 scores differing from the main table, so these cannot be interpreted as same-setting improvements.

T1.justification: The existing input/output mappings and binary reward definitions are retained. The multitask addition is procedural, with no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical guarantee. The additional mathematical reasoning traces are empirical case examples.

C1.justification: v1 centers on separately trained 8B/70B pairwise and pointwise judges. v2 makes a unified multitask judge a central contribution, claims superiority over separately trained counterparts, and extends its main performance claims to 32B models and comparisons with o3. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are revised around these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds the interpretation that multitask training combines pairwise comparative context with pointwise position consistency. It explicitly contrasts random-order and position-consistent accuracy, discusses decoding robustness, and expands interpretation of generated feedback. These extend the existing explanations of bias and score distributions without substantially revising their underlying account.

D1.justification: v2 discloses the synthetic preference-generation prompt in Figure 14 and a worked training-pair example in Table 5. Appendix C adds Qwen-specific hardware and sampling information, including 32 A100 GPUs and temperature 0.6. Existing training hyperparameters and judge prompt templates are largely retained, and a reproducibility statement is added.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Qwen3, o3, Reward Reasoning Model, CompassJudger, Atla, and RISE, and incorporates multitask learning into its novelty positioning. It removes the Wang et al. self-consistency citation. The broader positioning around generative reward models and online RL remains; publication updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract and contribution narrative, consolidates the method into three subsections, and reorganizes the results around PPE Correctness and multitask evaluation. It adds a qualitative-analysis discussion and reproducibility statement, introduces a thinking-traces appendix, and reorganizes the existing appendices.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the document template, removes v1's opening benchmark bar chart, updates the method diagram for multitasking, and redraws the score-distribution figure for the new model. It adds reasoning-trace displays and tables, restructures benchmark tables with Overall columns and gain annotations, and substantially reflows appendix prompts and results.

improvement.justification: The multitask comparisons, additional backbone, eight-seed decoding study, and data-generation documentation strengthen the paper. However, v2 newly claims RewardBench superiority at 93.6 despite retaining EvalPlanner's 93.8 in Table 2. Its new scalar-control table also reports unexplained J1 scores inconsistent with the main results. These conflicts affect important added comparisons, preventing a reliable judgment that the substantive benefits yield a net overall quality improvement.
